title: AI agents are checking the scientific literature — and spotting decades-old errors
excerpt: The technology is proving adept at finding faults in decades-old papers and reference databases.
content_html:
For decades, chemists have relied on handbook values for a molecule’s boiling point to identify substances and plan processes such as distillation. But an artificial-intelligence model has revealed that some trusted numbers in one reference database have been wrong all along.

Sebastian Pios, a theoretical chemist at Zhejiang Lab in Hangzhou, China, was using an AI system to predict the boiling points of several molecules when it began producing values that clashed with long-accepted entries in a 75-year-old reference database. At first, he thought the model was wrong. But when he manually checked the original literature, he found that the reference data were wrong, not the AI model.

In two other cases, Pios’s AI model spotted errors in older papers and reference books — mistakes that have made their way into the scientific canon. One was a typo in a paper; another was incorrect values of century-old boiling-point measurements. Both errors are likely to have caused researchers using the database “a lot of trouble”, says Pios.

Pios is one of a growing number of scientists using AI as a tool for auditing scientific knowledge. As well as checking databases, researchers are using specialized AI tools to hunt for errors in papers published in journals and conferences.

AI, peer review and the human activity of science

In an analysis posted online on 22 July, researchers at SAI Labs, a for-profit research-review company in Delaware, used AI agents to assess 168 papers selected for oral presentation at the 2026 International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML). The AI agents extracted the authors’ central claims, downloaded accompanying resources, reran experiments where possible and compared the results with those reported by the authors.

Of the 92 papers that had at least five claims available for assessment, the AI agents were able to reproduce more than two of the five claims from only 34 papers. The agents successfully repeated more than 80% of claims from just eight papers.

But such AI fact-checking tools remain unreliable arbiters of the scientific corpus, says Odd Erik Gundersen, a computer scientist at the Norwegian University of Science and Technology in Trondheim. The tools “make mistakes like humans do”, he says, which is why the quality of AI fact checkers must be processed manually with human oversight.

AI fact checker

Many researchers already dedicate their time to spotting errors in papers and use tools to check certain facets of papers. But one advantage of using AI is the speed at which it can scan scientific databases and literature compared with humans, says James Zou, a computer scientist at Stanford University, California. “The biggest difference is to be able to do this at a scale that was not possible before.”

In a study posted on the preprint server arXiv1, Zou and his colleagues used an ‘AI checker’ to scan papers published at NeurIPS — a prestigious annual AI research conference — for errors. Their tool found that errors in papers rose from 3.8 in 2021 to 5.9 in 2025 — an increase of 55%.

AI tools are spotting errors in research papers: inside a growing movement

“These are papers that have been published, so they’re sort of taken as the foundational knowledge for the next generation of research,” says Zou. “If there are mistakes in these foundations, this can propagate and make the follow-on research shakier,” he adds.

The analysis focused on ‘objective’ errors, such as those in formulae, calculations and figures, and excluded subjective mistakes about data interpretation and novelty. Co-author Federico Bianchi, a machine-learning scientist at Together AI, based in San Francisco, California, says this was a design choice. “AI should not do everything, and leave choices about novelty and significance to humans,” he says.

在另外两个案例中，皮奥斯的人工智能模型发现了旧论文和参考书中的错误——这些错误已经进入了科学经典。 其中一个是论文中的拼写错误；另一个原因是已有百年历史的沸点测量值不正确。 皮奥斯说，这两个错误都可能给研究人员使用数据库带来“很多麻烦”。

皮奥斯是越来越多使用人工智能作为审核科学知识工具的科学家之一。 除了检查数据库外，研究人员还使用专门的人工智能工具来寻找期刊和会议上发表的论文中的错误。

人工智能、同行评审和人类科学活动

在 7 月 22 日在线发布的一份分析中，特拉华州一家营利性研究评论公司 SAI Labs 的研究人员使用 AI 代理评估了 168 篇在 2026 年国际机器学习会议 (ICML) 上进行口头报告的论文。 人工智能代理提取了作者的核心主张，下载了随附资源，在可能的情况下重新进行实验，并将结果与​​作者报告的结果进行比较。

在至少有 5 项可供评估的主张的 92 篇论文中，人工智能代理仅能够从 34 篇论文中重现这 5 项主张中的超过两项。 代理人成功地重复了仅八篇论文中 80% 以上的主张。

但特隆赫姆挪威科技大学计算机科学家奥德·埃里克·冈德森 (Odd Erik Gundersen) 表示，此类人工智能事实核查工具仍然不是科学语料库的可靠仲裁者。 他说，这些工具“会像人类一样犯错误”，这就是为什么人工智能事实检查器的质量必须在人类监督下手动处理。

人工智能事实检查器

许多研究人员已经投入时间来发现论文中的错误并使用工具来检查论文的某些方面。 但加州斯坦福大学计算机科学家 James Zou 表示，使用人工智能的一个优势是，与人类相比，它扫描科学数据库和文献的速度更快。 “最大的区别是能够以以前不可能的规模做到这一点。”

在预印本服务器 arXiv1 上发布的一项研究中，Zou 和他的同事使用“人工智能检查器”扫描在 NeurIPS（著名的年度人工智能研究会议）上发表的论文是否存在错误。 他们的工具发现，论文错误从 2021 年的 3.8 个增加到 2025 年的 5.9 个，增加了 55%。

人工智能工具正在发现研究论文中的错误：在不断发展的运动中

“这些都是已经发表的论文，所以它们可以被视为下一代研究的基础知识，”邹说。 他补充道：“如果这些基础存在错误，这种错误就会传播开来，并使后续研究变得更加不稳定。”

分析的重点是“客观”错误，例如公式、计算和图表中的错误，并排除了有关数据解释和新颖性的主观错误。 合著者费德里科·比安奇 (Federico Bianchi) 是加利福尼亚州旧金山 Together AI 的机器学习科学家，他表示这是一个设计选择。 “人工智能不应该做所有事情，而把关于新颖性和重要性的选择留给人类，”他说。
